The Kentucky warbler (Geothlypis formosa) is a Neotropical migrant that breeds in the mature deciduous forests of the eastern United States. Eggs maintained at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C] in controlled laboratory settings hatch after approximately 12.5 days [ab = approximately 12.5 days], a duration that aligns well with incubation lengths reported for congeners of similar egg mass. The freshly laid egg has an initial wet weight of only 2.07 grams [Ww0 = 2.07 grams], reflecting the limited nutrient reserves available to the developing embryo before exogenous feeding begins. Field studies indicate that under a body temperature typical of active adults, 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], females lay 4 to 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 to 6 eggs per clutch] and produce a single brood each year [F_R_i = single brood each year], a modest reproductive output consistent with other ground-nesting Parulidae.

Neonatal mass at hatching provides a critical baseline for assessing postnatal growth trajectories in this species. Upon pipping, the hatchling wet weight averages 2.8 grams [Wwb = 2.8 grams], representing a modest increase over the initial egg mass and suggesting efficient conversion of albumen and yolk into embryonic tissue during the 12.5-day incubation period at 36 °C. This value places Kentucky warbler hatchlings among the lighter-bodied wood-warblers, a trait that likely influences the intensity and duration of parental provisioning during the nestling stage. The rapid mass gain that follows hatching is fueled by frequent feeding visits from both parents, who deliver protein-rich insect prey to the developing chicks. The nestlings undergo a period of accelerated growth that culminates in a series of well-defined developmental milestones.

At a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the fledging period marks a critical transition from nest dependence to initial flight capability. The time since birth at fledging is approximately 9.5 days [tx = approximately 9.5 days], a relatively short interval for an altricial passerine of this body size, likely an adaptation to reduce nest at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]predation risk. The downy chicks develop pin feathers within days, and by day eight they are capable of brief fluttering movements within the nest cup. Sexual maturation occurs later, reflecting the need for continued somatic growth and the acquisition of adult plumage before reproductive effort can be initiated. Under the same thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 28.5 days [tp = approximately 28.5 days], a marker of the onset of gonadal development.

Age at first reproduction is a key life-history parameter that influences population growth rates in migratory songbirds. For Kentucky warblers, under a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days], meaning that most individuals do not breed until their second calendar year, after returning from their first wintering season in Central America and the Caribbean. This deferred breeding is likely a consequence of the time required to acquire a high-quality territory in the densely populated understory habitat, as well as the energetic demands of a complete pre-basic molt. The species exhibits moderate sexual size dimorphism, with adult males generally attaining a larger asymptotic mass. The ultimate wet weight for adult males is 14.25 grams [Wwi = 14.25 grams], while females typically reach a slightly lower adult body mass of 14.2 grams [Wwi = 14.2 grams], a pattern that may reflect sex-specific energetic investments in territorial defense versus egg production.

Longevity data for this species come primarily from mark-recapture studies and banding records. At a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for Kentucky warblers is 7 years [am = 7 years], observed in a small number of individuals that survived multiple migration cycles and breeding seasons. This lifespan is typical for a small-bodied Parulid and reflects the cumulative mortality risks associated with long-distance migration, overwintering in tropical regions, and nesting on or near the forest floor. When considered against the age at first reproduction of 365 days and the annual reproductive output of 4 to 6 eggs per year, this relatively low annual fecundity places the Kentucky warbler at the slower end of the life-history continuum among North American warblers, a strategy that likely evolved in response to stable, mature forest environments with consistent but not abundant food resources.
